I doubt I'll be able to see anything, but I want an accurate estimate of whether the Moon is visible right now.

I'm in Denver, Colorado, USA at 2026-01-11 01:33 MST (UTC-0700) (2026-01-11T08:33:00Z in UTC), at latitude 39.7392 degrees and longitude -104.9903 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -64.305 degrees and its azimuth is 51.551 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 3.749 degrees and its azimuth is 113.235 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 43.46 percent illuminated, 82.321 degrees from the Sun, and 401200.6 kilometers away. The sky brightness is night, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—**you’d probably be able to spot it**, but it would be a difficult, low-altitude observation.

- The Moon is only **3.75° above the horizon**, so buildings, trees, terrain, haze, and atmospheric extinction could easily hide it. In Denver, the southeast horizon may also be obstructed depending on your exact location.
- At **43% illumination** and an angular separation of **82° from the Sun**, it is not in bright twilight; the dark sky provides good contrast.
- Its phase is likely a **waning crescent**, so it should still be reasonably bright—far brighter than most stars.
- At that altitude, atmospheric extinction and turbulence will make it look dimmer, reddish, and possibly distorted. The quoted distance makes it somewhat smaller and fainter than average, but not dramatically so.

**Practical estimate:** from a location with a genuinely clear, unobstructed southeast horizon, perhaps a **good chance—around 70–90%**—if you know the correct direction. From an ordinary urban or suburban viewpoint, the chance may drop to **30–60%**, mainly because something near the horizon will block it or haze will wash it out.

Look toward **azimuth 113°**—roughly east-southeast—only about **four finger-widths above a perfectly level horizon**. Binoculars can help you locate it, but don’t scan near the horizon with them unless you are certain the Sun is safely below it; at the stated time the Sun is far enough below the horizon that this is not a practical concern.
